According to Duffy's November 14 briefing:
1. FAA contractor L3Harris Technologies was doing routine maintenance at a remote FAA facility, replacing an obsolete copper telecommunications connection with fiber.
2. A newly installed router began flooding other air traffic control routers with over 1,000 connection attempts every 4-5 seconds.
3. That connection storm overwhelmed legacy equipment, causing intermittent radar-feed and voice-communication problems.
4. The FAA isolated the maintenance work, restored the systems and reopened the airspace.

Screenshot of Timberborn, a beaver city-builder, seen from a high isometric angle over a voxel landscape of terraced brown cliffs, green grassy patches, and dark still ponds, with pale blue sky at the top left.

Center foreground: a raised plateau packed with a dense grid of roughly forty pale wooden windmills, linked by power lines on tall poles that run across the map. A row of long, low storage buildings lines its right edge. A barrel-shaped tank and a small domed building with a glowing green top sit at its left. Staircases climb the cliff faces below, and a dark, grass-rimmed pond sits at the bottom of the frame.

Upper left: a huge rectangular basin dug into the terrain, with stepped inner walls, a shallow pool, and a grid of walkways crossing its floor. Beside it is a second, sparser array of windmills.

Upper right: the main settlement. It has clusters of round-roofed wooden houses, white multistory buildings, a tall white domed tower, and a stacked multi-tier platform crowded with more windmills. Around it are golden and green crop fields, a dark green tree plantation, rows of crops on reddish soil, and water channels winding between terraces.

Right foreground: a tall wooden scaffold outlined in orange, a building under construction, next to an orange-outlined empty plot. The left foreground is barren, cracked earth dotted with dry pale grass. The map's edge drops off into blue at the bottom-left corner.

I seem to have empirically eliminated DoS bugs from my web server as a category by instructing ChatGPT to write a profiler to find every single location in the code along the request path that a DoS could even theoretically occur because it's a resource that an attacker could control, and then test it under load with the deployment benchmark tests so it simulates real web apps, and then go through all of the resulting 3000 locations by hand and put them into categories/clusters, then further categorize them as potential DoSes or not, then make a giant formal resource ledger based on the profiling results of every single data structure in the request path and prove that these cannot be pushed into a state that DoSes the server, during which I watched it go through and find the remaining DoS flaws after the ledger flagged their potential to exist and patch them all.

The vision I got from Democritus was of a God who was single-mindedly obsessed with enforcing a couple of rules about certain types of information you are not allowed to have under any circumstances. Some of these rules I’d already known about. You can’t have information from outside your light cone. You can’t have information about the speed and position of a particle at the same time. Others I hadn’t thought about as much until reading Democritus. Information about when a Turing machine will halt. Information about whether certain formal systems are consistent. Precise information about the quantum state of a particle. The reason God hasn’t solved world poverty yet is that He is pacing about feverishly worried that someone, somewhere, is going to be able to measure the quantum state of a particle too precisely, and dreaming up new and increasingly bizarre ways He can prevent that from happening.

And yes, it’s a magic item. Here’s the stat block:

Pods of the Quiet Sphere
Wondrous item (pair), rare (requires attunement, via Bluetooth)

While wearing these, you may speak the command word “noise control” to wrap yourself in a 30-foot sphere of silence. No concentration required; cannot be dispelled. The silence is subjective: creatures outside the sphere can hear you just fine, and they will notice if you sing.

The pods hold 6 charges of daylight and regain all of them when returned to their small white reliquary. If separated from the wearer, one pod will invariably roll beneath the nearest couch.

Curse: once per long rest, the pods will connect to the wrong device.

Phone screenshot of a document titled “index” in a cream-colored reading view. Large serif heading: “Oh, Interesting.” Italic subtitle: “A few things Kylee’s 23andMe file says, picked for surprise rather than completeness. Not medical. Nothing scary on purpose.”

First card: “The caffeine thing,” with a gold tag reading “Half a story.” Gene labels: ADORA2A rs5751876 CC · CYP1A2 rs762551 AC. Text: “Her liver gene for clearing caffeine is boringly intermediate, so her liver isn’t the answer. The interesting part is the receptor that caffeine actually plugs into. The version linked to caffeine anxiety is TT. She’s CC, the opposite end. So: caffeine probably doesn’t make her jittery, and that’s in her genes. Whether it keeps her awake is murkier. The sleep studies disagree about which version is the sensitive one. The venti-then-nap trick is still partly a mystery.”

Second card, cut off at the bottom: “Cilantro,” with a green tag reading “Fits,” and the label near OR6A2 rs72921001 AA. A share button overlaps its top corner.
